paragraphs.source_en: In contrast with the Pleistocene, the Holocene is supported by a large number of radiocarbon dates, showing an almost continuous occupation of the Central Sahara from circa 10,000 to 2,000 BP. Two Early Holocene cultural phases, namely the Epipalaeolithic dating from 10,000 to 8,800 BP and the Mesolithic dating from 8,800 to 7,400 BP, are quite similar regarding the subsistence strategies which were based exclusively on wild animals. In the Epipalaeolithic 90% of the faunal remains are represented by mouflon, whereas the Mesolithic period presents a wider range of hunted animals, prevalently small ones. The lithic industry in both phases shows continuity but in the earlier phase microlithics clearly prevail whereas there was an increase in the production of macrolithic tools in the later phase.

paragraphs.source_en: Grinding stones are very rare in the Epipalaeolithic, however their numbers increase greatly in the Mesolithic phase. The two phases therefore present a strong homogeneity of hunter-gatherers occupying the shelters for more than 2,000 years and adopting new elements and technologies according to the changing climatic and environmental conditions (Di Lernia 1996).

paragraphs.source_en: The different tool typology prevailing in each phase is likely to reflect different use of resources. Fishing seems to have been indicated by the presence of microlithic tools, whose functional interpretation appears related to fishing activity (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1998). The scarcity of organic finds in this older layer is explained by a more humid period than the successive layer, although the wettest period preceded the very first occupation of the shelters (Castelletti, et al. 1998). The Epipalaeolithic was still rich in water and in flora requiring more periodical rains than the Mesolithic phase (Mercuri 1999). Such a humid environment not only attracted abundant fauna, but also provided the best conditions for waterdependent animals.
